source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 5 (Genetics), sections covering the genus Oryza and indica/japonica classification. No elibrary URL visible.
text: Background genetics reference on rice classification (useful context for understanding variety breeding, not a farming technique itself). The genus Oryza contains 22 recognized wild and cultivated species (citing Vaughan, 1994), including O. schlechteri, O. brachyantha, O. longiglumis, O. ridleyi, O. granulate, O. meyeriana, O. minuta, O. officinalis, O. rhizomatis, O. eichingeri, O. punctata, O. latifolia, O. alta, O. grandiglumis, O. australiensis, O. meridionalis, O. rufipogon, O. nivara, O. sativa, O. longistaminata, O. barthii, and O. glaberrima. Of these, Oryza sativa (Asian rice) is the species cultivated in Cambodia and across most of Asia; O. glaberrima (African rice) is a separately-domesticated species grown in West Africa. Within O. sativa, two major subspecies are recognized: indica and japonica, historically distinguished by grain shape and geography but confirmed genetically via isozyme analysis. A cold-tolerance study (Oka, 1999) found that indica-type rice tolerates temperatures above about 13 degrees C during a sensitive growth stage without sterility damage, while japonica-type rice can tolerate temperatures below 13 degrees C at the same stage - a genetic basis for indica's dominance in Cambodia's tropical lowlands versus japonica's use in cooler/higher-altitude or temperate rice-growing regions. A finer genetic classification scheme (Glaszmann, 1987, based on isozyme groups) divides cultivated rice into six groups: Group I is broadly equivalent to indica; Group II corresponds to javanica-type rice; Groups III, IV, and V represent additional indica-type variation; and Group VI corresponds to 'aus' rice, a very-early-maturity group grown mainly in South Asia (e.g. Bangladesh).
